methodologyNote: Accuracy-first educational museum seed. Prefer null over invention. Every specification carries a confidence tag. No operational targeting, construction recipes, or lethality-optimization content.

description.en: Twin-engine, two-seat air-superiority fighter. Iran is the only foreign customer. Ordered under Project Persian King in 1974 and delivered from 1976, Iranian Tomcats retained AWG-9 radar and AIM-54 Phoenix capability. After 1979 and the U.S. embargo, IRIAF sustained a reduced fleet through domestic maintenance and flew them extensively in the Iran–Iraq War.

historicalContext.en: Selected partly to counter high-altitude Soviet MiG-25 overflights. Contracts covered 80 aircraft; sources agree 79 were delivered and the 80th retained in the United States.

technologicalSignificance.en: Only non-U.S. Tomcat operator; AWG-9/Phoenix suite drove decades of Iranian sustainment effort.

variants.name: F-14A-GR (Iran export configuration)
variants.notes: Some ECM differences vs USN reported.

operators: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force
disputedClaims: Individual Iran–Iraq War aerial victory tallies.
systems.notes: Stress unique export status and embargo-era sustainment rather than unverified kill counts.

description.en: Cornerstone fighter-bomber of IIAF/IRIAF. Iran received F-4D, large numbers of F-4E, and RF-4E reconnaissance aircraft before 1979. After the embargo, IRIAF kept Phantoms flying through Mehrabad depot overhaul and domestic parts programs.

historicalContext.en: First F-4Ds late 1960s; F-4Es from 1971 under Peace Roll FMS. Flew deep strike and air combat in the Iran–Iraq War; remain in service into the 21st century.

technologicalSignificance.en: Long-term industrial adaptation: structural repair, cannibalization, and selective avionics/weapons integration on a Cold War U.S. airframe.

specifications.notes: Key.Aero Phantom Survivors; final batches cancelled by embargo.

operators: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force
systems.notes: Do not invent upgrade performance claims.

systems.manufacturer: Northrop; later Iranian modernization by IAMI/HESA

description.en: Light fighter and lead-in trainer that equipped multiple IIAF/IRIAF squadrons. After the embargo, Iran kept F-5E/F airworthy and launched domestic upgrade lines (Kowsar) and visually modified derivatives (Saeqeh).

historicalContext.en: Tiger IIs replaced earlier F-5A/B types mid-1970s. Fought in Iran–Iraq War; remain in training and secondary roles. June 2020 ceremonies handed over Kowsar-upgraded F-5Fs.

technologicalSignificance.en: Baseline for Iran’s most visible indigenous fighter derivatives; distinguish imported F-5s from later modified projects.

operators: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force
disputedClaims: How much of Kowsar is new-manufacture versus remanufacture.
systems.notes: Baseline originType is imported; label derivatives separately.

systems.manufacturer: Bell Helicopter; Iranian overhaul/upgrade by IHSRC/Panha and IAMI

description.en: Twin-engine attack helicopter purchased as AH-1J International. Primary operator is Iranian Army Aviation (Havanirooz/IRIAA), not IRIAF. A minority of the original fleet was TOW-capable. Post-embargo overhauls/upgrades include Panha 2091/Toufan.

historicalContext.en: Pre-1979 purchase commonly cited as 202 aircraft (62 TOW-capable). Heavily used against Iraqi armor early in the Iran–Iraq War. IRGC Army Aviation later obtained a small number.

technologicalSignificance.en: Shows Iran’s rotary-wing sustainment ecosystem and incremental indigenous modernization of an embargoed U.S. type.

relations.note: TOW/Toophan family associated with TOW-capable Cobras.

operators: Islamic Republic of Iran Army Aviation
systems.notes: CORRECTED: brief said IRIAF, but sources place AH-1J with Army Aviation (IRIAA) and limited IRGC aviation—not IRIAF.

description.en: Medium-range semi-active radar-homing SAM. Imperial Iranian Air Force bought Improved HAWK batteries under PEACE SHIELD FMS in 1972. After 1979 suspension of U.S. support, Iran maintained HAWK equipment and later fielded Mersad using Shahin/Shalamcheh missiles derived from HAWK technology.

historicalContext.en: U.S. Army Redstone chronology: July 1972 FMS for 24 Improved HAWK batteries (nearly USD 280 million); formal suspension 4 November 1979. Iran Watch: Mersad declared operational April 2010.

technologicalSignificance.en: Imported Western SAM architecture later reverse-engineered into Iranian Mersad family.

specifications.notes: Iranian MoD announcement via Iran Watch.

operators: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Defense Force
disputedClaims: Remaining original HAWK hardware vs indigenous Mersad inventories.
systems.notes: Separate PEACE SHIELD import era from post-2010 Mersad family on labels.

description.en: British MBT with 120 mm L11 gun. Iran was the largest export customer, receiving Mk 3P/5P and improved FV4030/1 before 1979. Shir 1 (FV4030/2) and Shir 2 (FV4030/3) orders were cancelled after the Revolution; undelivered Shir designs fed Jordan’s Khalid and Britain’s Challenger 1. Mobarez is an Iranian upgrade name for surviving Chieftains—not a UK export model. Specific Mobarez performance data remain poorly documented.

historicalContext.en: Open references commonly state 707 Mk 3P/5P MBTs plus 187 FV4030/1, with ARV/AVLB support vehicles. Chieftains fought in the Iran–Iraq War with mixed results constrained by automotive reliability.

technologicalSignificance.en: Documents UK–Iran armored relationship, aborted Shir program influence on Challenger, and Iranian renaming of modernized foreign armor.

specifications.notes: Royal Ordnance L11 rifled gun (baseline Chieftain).
Open claims (~850 hp) insufficiently sourced for confirmation.

description.en: Tracked IFV. Iran acquired BMP-1s during/after the Iran–Iraq War through multiple reported channels and later operated Chinese Type 86 vehicles. Iran also developed the Boragh family influenced by BMP-1/Type 86 design.

historicalContext.en: Secondary operator lists report Syrian and Soviet/Czechoslovak supply routes in the 1980s plus Chinese copies. Exact import batches remain uncertain.

technologicalSignificance.en: Introduced mechanized IFV concepts into Iranian ground forces and informed later Boragh production.

specifications.notes: Baseline Soviet design; Iranian local mods may differ.

description.en: Export MBT associated with T-72B-standard features. Iran signed a November 1991 agreement with Russia covering T-72S production licensing and also received complete tanks while facilities were built. Assembly at Dorud reportedly began 8 July 1997; first Iranian-produced examples entered service July 1998. Separately, Iran obtained earlier T-72M1 export tanks—do not conflate T-72M1 and T-72S.

historicalContext.en: Part of post-war rearmament after attrition of Western armor. Ambitious license totals in some accounts appear unfulfilled; treat large planned figures cautiously.

technologicalSignificance.en: Shift from purely imported Western MBTs toward licensed Soviet/Russian production and local industrial support.

specifications.notes: GlobalSecurity figure; confirm before exhibit label.

variants.notes: Earlier export T-72A-derived model; imported separately.

description.en: Early Iranian tactical reconnaissance UAV used in the Iran–Iraq War for battlefield photography and artillery spotting. Twin-boom pusher layout with fixed landing gear; short-range radio control without mature autopilot.

historicalContext.en: Among Iran’s first series-produced drones. Iranian press retrospectives credit Mohajer imagery in late-war operations; treat exact sortie statistics cautiously.

technologicalSignificance.en: Foundational ISR UAV that seeded the later Mohajer family.

specifications.notes: Open figures vary widely; do not present a single number as fact.

description.en: Improved tactical ISR UAV with autopilot, composite airframe, and real-time imagery downlink versus Mohajer-1. Jane's Unmanned (2014–15) is the principal specialist reference for published dimensions and endurance.

historicalContext.en: Widely fielded after the Iran–Iraq War; later license-assembled in Venezuela as Arpia. Mohajer-2N (2014) is an electronics/performance refresh.

technologicalSignificance.en: Matured Iranian tactical UAV practice: waypoint autopilot, catapult launch, exportable ISR package.

description.en: Larger evolutionary Mohajer ISR UAV with greater endurance and payload flexibility than Mohajer-2. Used by multiple Iranian services and observed with partners abroad. Mohajer-4B (Sadiq) is a later airframe refresh.

historicalContext.en: Entered service around the late 1990s per specialist summaries; documented in regional conflicts in the 2010s as an ISR asset.

technologicalSignificance.en: Bridges early wartime drones and later armed Mohajer-6 designs while remaining primarily ISR in baseline form.

specifications.notes: Commonly cited; confirm against Jane's before final label.

disputedClaims: Whether Hodhod/Shahin labels are true subvariants or nicknames.
systems.notes: Mohajer-6 is a later armed family member; not expanded here.

systems.developer: HESA / earlier program histories differ (Qods vs IEI)

description.en: Multirole tactical UAV family. Early Ababil-1 is poorly documented. Ababil-2 (publicly revealed 1999) serves as target drone, rudimentary surveillance, and twin-tail attack/loitering variants. Ababil-3 is a larger twin-boom ISR redesign from the 2000s. Jane's Unmanned is the best specialist baseline for Ababil-2 data.

historicalContext.en: Program start dates differ between Jane's (Qods, 1986; delivery 1993) and other analysts (IEI mid-1980s). Widely observed in the region under various local names.

technologicalSignificance.en: Among Iran’s most widely proliferated tactical UAV families; modular mission payloads on simple airframes.

description.en: Road-mobile, single-stage, solid-propellant short-range ballistic missile. Marks Iran’s move from liquid-fuel Scud/Shahab lineage toward indigenous solid-fuel tactical missiles. Secondary literature discusses conceptual links to Zelzal solid-rocket experience and earlier short-range systems including CSS-8/Tondar-69 discussions.

historicalContext.en: Wisconsin Project summarizes Iranian claims of domestic solid-propellant ingredient production around 2000, flight tests in 2001–2002, and a mass-production plant announcement in 2002. Later generation range/guidance claims should be labeled carefully.

technologicalSignificance.en: Milestone in Iranian solid-fuel SRBM engineering and road-mobile tactical missile logistics.

specifications.notes: Common early figure; some sources ~170 km—mark disputed.
Iranian/media generation claims; not independently confirmed in this seed.

systems.notes: HISTORICAL/TECHNICAL ONLY. No targeting or employment doctrines.

description.en: Iranian long-range SAM publicly framed as an indigenous counterpart to long-range Russian systems after S-300 delivery difficulties. Prototype shown 2016; official induction August 2019. Architecture includes search/engagement radars and vertical canister launchers with Sayyad-family missiles. Many performance figures remain official claims without independent verification.

historicalContext.en: CSIS Missile Threat: officials claimed tracking up to 60 targets and max engagement 250 km at induction. Washington Institute 2023 table lists differing higher claimed figures including up to 300 km—label Disputed.

technologicalSignificance.en: Most ambitious publicly displayed Iranian LR-SAM; high uncertainty on true performance.

specifications.notes: Official claim at induction (CSIS). Other claims 200–300 km.

relations.note: Part of broader Iranian layered SAM evolution, not a HAWK derivative.

operators: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Defense Force (claimed)
systems.notes: Prefer 'claimed' language on all visitor labels.

systems.originCountry: France (Kaman/Combattante II parent); Iran (Sina domestic builds)
systems.developer: Based on French Combattante II / Iranian reverse-engineered production

description.en: Missile-armed fast attack craft. Original Kaman boats were French Combattante II hulls delivered 1974–1981. Sina class is an Iranian-built near-copy/reverse-engineered continuation, armed with C-802/Noor-family anti-ship missiles and a 76 mm gun. Related small craft such as Peykaap (IPS-16) are a different North Korean–linked high-speed lineage and should not be conflated with Sina.

historicalContext.en: Two Kaman boats lost in 1980 and 1988. Iranian industry launched domestic Sina units named after lost Kaman boats (Paykan, Joshan). Iranian media sometimes call them frigates; displacement reporting places them as FAC/missile boats.

technologicalSignificance.en: Example of reverse-engineered Western FAC production and missile substitution (Harpoon to Noor/C-802 family).

specifications.notes: Common Combattante II/Kaman figure; some Sina reports cite ~350 t.

disputedClaims: Exact displacement of later Sina units.
systems.notes: Peykaap documented in sources (src-globalsecurity-peykaap) for future expansion; origin disputed (indigenous claim vs NK delivery).

systems.developer: Hughes/US TOW lineage; Iranian defense industry for Toophan
systems.introductionPeriod: Toophan-1 often dated late 1980s in secondary literature

description.en: Iranian family of tube-launched, wire-guided anti-tank missiles derived from the U.S. BGM-71 TOW. Pre-1979 U.S.–Iran industrial cooperation included TOW-related licensed production pathways that did not continue as a full enduring license after the Revolution. Post-1979 production is best characterized as reverse engineering and indigenous development on that incomplete licensed base. Toophan-1 corresponds closely to early TOW; later variants are Iranian evolutions.

historicalContext.en: ARES/SADJ traces the family to 1970s licensed TOW efforts and subsequent Iranian variants. FRUS documents provide primary-context evidence of 1970s co-production discussions.

technologicalSignificance.en: Key case for nuanced origin typing: incomplete licensed pathway plus reverse engineering.

specifications.notes: MOD export webpage claims via ARES/SADJ—not independently verified.

operators: other regional users documented by researchers
disputedClaims: Whether Toophan-1 should be labeled licensed_production vs reverse_engineered (seed uses reverse_engineered with licensed-pathway note).
systems.notes: originType reverse_engineered with explicit licensed-pathway nuance in description.

description.en: Pre-modern seed exhibit on indigenous Iranian production of cannon and muskets, anchored in Encyclopaedia Iranica’s peer academic articles on firearms history and manufacture. Intended as a museum bridge between early modern Persian military technology and twentieth-century systems—without inventing caliber lists or production numbers until full Iranica text is incorporated by curators.

historicalContext.en: Iranica’s FIREARMS entries survey how gunpowder weapons were produced and adopted in Iranian polities. Complementary museum scholarship can expand object-level labels later.

technologicalSignificance.en: Establishes long-run continuity of Iranian arms manufacture for the historical gallery.
